text.story:
The homework is finished.
The pencil is down.
Pip still wants to snap it.

He pushes the book away. It bumps his comic, sliding it halfway across the table. He wanted to read it, but opening it feels like more work.

Dad sits beside him. “The work is done, but you still look bothered.” He leaves the book. Pip presses his palms against the table and stares at the cover.

“I'm mad,” Pip says. Then he shakes his head. “Except not exactly. Can you help me find the word? I don't want help with the homework. It's already finished.”

“We can look for the feeling's name,” Dad says. “I'll offer guesses, but you get to say whether they fit.” Pip nudges the comic back into line with the table edge.

“Annoyed?” Dad asks. “Disappointed?” Pip rolls his pencil. Neither word sounds quite right on its own. He wants a word that includes all the rubbing out, and the time that seemed to disappear.

“I knew what I wanted to do,” Pip says. “But I kept getting stuck halfway through. Like pushing a door that won't open, except the door is a question about numbers.”

“Frustrated might fit that stuck feeling,” Dad says. Pip stops rolling the pencil. That word has the right sort of edges. “Yes. Frustrated,” he says. “But there's another bit underneath.”

“It's more than mad,” Pip says. He picks up his speech bubble eraser. For something shaped like talking, it has remarkably little to say. He holds it toward Dad, who waits without supplying its speech.

Pip puts it down. “Can you give me the whole practice?” Dad nods and says:

“Think of one small thing that bugged you this week. Say the first word that comes. Probably bad, or mad. Now find a sharper word. Annoyed? Embarrassed? Left out? Let down? Jealous? Nervous? Pick one. If two fit, say both. Say it out loud: 'I felt embarrassed, and a bit annoyed.' Now give it a number from 1 to 10. That's it. The word is a tool, not a grade.”

Pip looks at the comic. He thought there would be a long stretch of reading after homework. Instead, that stretch feels squeezed. “Disappointed,” he says. “Because I wanted more time for this.”

“Two feelings fit,” Pip says. He touches his chest, and Dad touches his own. “I feel frustrated and disappointed.” Saying both feels more accurate than choosing one and leaving the other loose.

“Frustrated is seven. Disappointed is five,” Pip adds. Dad keeps listening. Pip checks the words against what he feels. He doesn't want to swap either one, even though he still wants to shove the book.

“Naming feelings has sometimes helped adults feel less upset,” Dad says quietly. “That doesn't tell us whether this practice helps children.” He leaves Pip room to notice his own answer.

“My shoulders are still all stiff,” Pip says. “But you know what I mean now.” Dad nods. “You found two words that fit, instead of making one word cover everything.”

Dad shifts his chair back as Pip opens the comic. Pip reads the same sentence twice. His thoughts keep catching on how long the homework took.

“Still frustrated,” Pip says. Dad stays beside him. Pip rests one hand on his chest and adds, “And disappointed.” Then he looks back at the page, with both feelings still there.

feelFirst: Finishing homework doesn't always finish the feeling.
It can be hard to find words for what's still bothering you.

tinyTryOptions.text: Choose a small bother. Touch your chest and say the feeling word that fits.
Let a grown-up offer feeling words. Say which fits, or choose your own.
If two feelings fit, say both. Give each a number from one to ten.

whereElse.line: Where else could you name a feeling?
whereElse.place: At the kitchen table with a grown-up.

text.replayCue: When everything feels bad, look for a feeling word that fits.
